To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) dopamine (DA) is necessary for motor learning; 2) the DA D1 receptor is critical for motor learning; and 3) DA D1 receptor activation in the striatum is critical for motor skill consolidation.

(i) DA is critical for motor learning, (ii) the DA‐dependent long‐duration response is critical for motor skill learning, (iii) the DA‐mediated long‐duration response depends on the corticostriatum, and (iv) the corticostrial DA‐mediated response is critical for the long‐duration motor skill response.
dopamine (DA)‐dependent motor learning and motor performance are dissociable and that the DA‐dependent motor learning is a prerequisite of DA‐dependent motor performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dopamine and its metabolites in the regulation of the motor behavior and the motor learning.
how the dopamine system contributes to motor learning.
the role of dopamine in the mediation of the effects of levodopa and other drugs on motor function, motor learning, cognitive processes, and corticocortical and cortico‐subcortical connectivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of the DA system in motor learning is to modulate the amount of motor output, but not the quality of the motor output.
dopamine plays an important role in motor learning.
dopamine is a neurotransmitter that has a role in learning, and that this learning is related to the motor function of an organism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

DA is critical for motor learning and performance, and that the long‐duration response of levodopa on motor learning may be due to the long‐lasting effect of levodopa in increasing DA levels in the striatum.
the long‐duration effect of L‐DOPA on motor learning is mediated through DA‐dependent modulation of corticostriatopallidal circuitry.
dopamine is critical for motor learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the motor performance and learning are not always coupled.
levodopa's effect on motor performance and motor learning is dependent on the level of DA.
DA is not only important in the expression of motor performance but also plays a role in learning, especially in the early stages of learning.
